business_model.basis: Stated directly in the 10-K Item 1 Business section.
business_model.claim: FirstEnergy sells regulated electricity—distribution, transmission, and generation services—to over six million customers across Ohio, Pennsylvania, West Virginia, Maryland, New Jersey, and New York.
quotes: FE and its subsidiaries are principally involved in the transmission, distribution, and generation of electricity.

The Electric Companies' combined service areas encompass approximately 65,000 square miles in Ohio, Pennsylvania, West Virginia, Maryland, New Jersey, and New York, providing distribution services for over six million customers in an area with a population of approximately 14 million and a total rate base of approximately $21.3 billion as of December 31, 2025.

business_model.basis: Stated directly in the 10-K Item 1 Business section.
business_model.claim: FirstEnergy reports three operating segments: Distribution (Ohio Companies and FE PA), Integrated (MP, PE, JCP&L), and Stand-Alone Transmission (FET and KATCo), plus a Corporate/Other bucket.
quotes: •Distribution Segment, which consists of the Ohio Companies and FE PA; •Integrated Segment, which consists of MP, PE and JCP&L; and •Stand-Alone Transmission Segment, which consists of FE's ownership in FET and KATCo.

business_model.basis: Stated directly in the 10-K Item 1 Business section.
business_model.claim: As of December 31, 2025, the three segments held rate bases of $11.1 billion (Distribution), $10.2 billion (Integrated), and $5.4 billion (Stand-Alone Transmission, FirstEnergy-owned).
quotes: FirstEnergy's Distribution segment, which consists of the Ohio Companies and FE PA, representing $11.1 billion in rate base as of December 31, 2025, distributes electricity through FirstEnergy's electric operating companies in Ohio and Pennsylvania.

FirstEnergy's Integrated segment includes the distribution and transmission operations of JCP&L, MP and PE, as well as MP's regulated generation operations, representing $10.2 billion in rate base as of December 31, 2025.

FirstEnergy's Stand-Alone Transmission segment, which consists of FE's ownership in FET and KATCo, representing $5.4 billion in FirstEnergy-owned rate base as of December 31, 2025, includes transmission infrastructure owned and operated by the Transmission Companies.

business_model.basis: Stated directly in the 10-K Item 1 Business section.

business_model.basis: Stated directly in the 10-Q MD&A Finance section.
business_model.claim: The $36 billion Energize365 capital plan for 2026–2030 is funded by organic cash flow, debt (including hybrid securities), and up to $2 billion of equity or equity-like securities, with approximately 1% of market cap in new common equity per year.
quotes: FirstEnergy's customer-focused Energize365 investment plan for 2026 to 2030 is $36 billion, approximately 25% higher than the previous 2025 to 2029 five-year plan, and aims to strengthen the grid, improve reliability and support growing customer demand.

Energize365 capital investments included in the current five-year plan are expected to be funded with a combination of organic cash flows and the issuance of debt, including hybrid securities. The financing plan for the current $36 billion 2026 to 2030 investment program includes up to $2 billion of equity or equity-like securities through 2030.

risks.basis: Stated in P4 (10-Q MD&A, Regulatory Matters – Maryland). The Act's text is summarized by management; the full statutory language is not in the evidence.
risks.claim: Maryland's Utility RELIEF Act, signed May 12, 2026, limits use of forecasted costs in rate proceedings, eliminates certain utility earnings incentives, and allocates transmission and distribution upgrade costs associated with data centers to those customers rather than the broader customer base, which may affect PE's timing and amount of cost recovery and future earnings opportunities.
quotes: the Utility RELIEF Act may affect PE's timing and amount of cost recovery, authorized returns, customer rate structures, infrastructure investment planning, and future earnings opportunities

eliminates certain utility earnings incentives, imposes restrictions on recovery of certain administrative compensation costs and includes provisions designed to allocate certain transmission and distribution upgrade costs associated with large-load customers, including data centers, to those customers rather than to the broader customer base

risks.basis: Stated in P2 (10-K Risk Factors). The FERC proceeding is described as 'considering,' not finalized, as of the 10-K filing date (February 2026). The 10-Q (P5) confirms no material change to risk factors as of September 30, 2026.
risks.claim: FERC is considering regulations to speed interconnection of AI data centers and large loads to the transmission system, with final regulations expected in the second quarter of 2026; if the rules do not permit transmission utilities to fully recover costs of network upgrades for large loads, FirstEnergy's transmission investment strategy could be adversely affected.
quotes: FERC, at the instruction of the U.S. Secretary of Energy, is also considering whether to develop regulations intended to speed interconnection of AI data centers and 'hybrid' data center/electric generation facilities (collectively, 'large loads') to the transmission system. Final regulations, if any, from FERC are expected in the second quarter of 2026.

To the extent the new regulations promulgated by FERC do not permit transmission utilities to fully recover costs associated with transmission network upgrades required to serve new large loads, our strategy of investing in transmission could be adversely affected.

risks.basis: The 16,985 MW figure and the explicit uncertainty statement are stated in P2 (10-K Risk Factors). The 8 GW contracted and 4 GW pipeline figures are stated in P4 (10-Q MD&A) and P6 (8-K earnings release). The 'cannot predict' language is the company's own risk disclosure.
risks.claim: FirstEnergy's long-term growth thesis depends on data center load growth (up to 16,985 MWs through 2035), with approximately 8 GWs contracted and approximately 4 GWs in active negotiations as of October 27, 2026; the company explicitly states it cannot predict whether the data centers under consideration will ever commence operations.
quotes: A need to serve the load obligations of these data centers, which could be up to 16,985 MWs through 2035, has the potential to adversely impact our business, results of operations, financial condition, or cash flows.
FirstEnergy cannot predict whether the data centers under consideration will ever commence operations or the size of the load obligations of those that do become operational.
As of October 27, 2026, FirstEnergy has contracted approximately 8 GWs of capacity and was in active negotiations concerning approximately 4 GWs of additional load.

risks.basis: Stated in P2 (10-K Risk Factors, 'External pressures beyond our control'). The January 16, 2026 PJM board action is described as expressing 'interest,' not a final decision.
risks.claim: PJM capacity auctions have cleared at all-time high prices subject to a price collar, and on January 16, 2026 the PJM board and federal and state officials expressed interest in extending the collar through mid-2030; if auctions continue to clear at the cap and a 'backstop' auction is conducted at a high price, customer resistance could lead regulators to limit capital investment in transmission and distribution.
quotes: PJM's recent capacity auctions have been subject to a 'price collar' that has resulted from all-time high generation capacity prices in recent auction outcomes. These all-time high capacity prices ultimately are passed through in retail rates and can result in material increases in retail customers' monthly electric utility bills.
On January 16, 2026, the PJM board along with various federal and state officials, expressed interest in extending the price collar through mid-2030.

customer resistance to the resulting market driven increases on the generation portion of their bills could lead to increased pressure for state and federal utility regulators to limit the needed capital investment in transmission and distribution systems required for safe, reliable and resilient service to customers, which may impair our ability to earn a fair and equitable return on our investments

risks.basis: Stated in P2 (10-K Risk Factors). The 'probable loss' language is the company's own accounting assessment. The inability to estimate a range means the magnitude is unknown.
risks.claim: The securities class action In re FirstEnergy Corp. Securities Litigation remains pending, and the company states it is probable that FE will incur a loss but cannot reasonably estimate the amount or range; the related DPA obligations continue until the January 2025 indictment of two former officers is resolved.
quotes: We believe that it is probable that FE will incur a loss in connection with the resolution of In re FirstEnergy Corp. Securities Litigation. Given the ongoing nature and complexity of such litigation, we cannot yet reasonably estimate a loss or range of loss that may arise from its resolution.

if it is resolved against us substantial monetary damages could result and our reputation, business, financial condition, results of operations, liquidity or cash flows may be materially adversely affected

risks.claim: FirstEnergy's balance sheet carries $2,156 million of currently payable long-term debt and $1,970 million of short-term borrowings (table in millions) as of September 30, 2026, alongside a $36 billion five-year capital plan to be funded by organic cash flows, debt issuance (including hybrids), and up to $2 billion of equity or equity-like securities through 2030; a tightening of capital markets or a significant rise in interest rates could constrain financing for the Energize365 program.

risks.basis: Stated in P2 (10-K Risk Factors, NERC/FERC reliability standards section). The $1.5 million per day figure is the statutory maximum, not an expected loss.
risks.claim: FERC retains authority to impose penalties up to $1.5 million per day for failure to comply with NERC mandatory reliability standards, and PJM may direct FirstEnergy's transmission affiliates to build new facilities to meet reliability requirements under the PJM Tariff, potentially at costs not fully recoverable in rates.
quotes: FERC has the authority under the FPA to impose penalties up to and including $1.5 million per day, subject thereafter to annual adjustments for inflation, for failure to comply with these mandatory reliability standards.
PJM may direct our transmission-owning affiliates to build new transmission facilities to meet PJM's reliability requirements or to provide new or expanded transmission service under the PJM Tariff.

risks.basis: Stated in P1 (10-K Item 1, Supply Chain section). The company's own assessment of no expected material impact is included in the same passage.
risks.claim: FirstEnergy's supply chain for grid equipment has not fully returned to pre-pandemic lead times amid increased industry demand (including data centers) and U.S. tariff actions; a prolonged continuation or increase in demand, or adverse macroeconomic conditions including inflationary pressures and new tariffs, could increase supply chain disruptions and adversely affect results of operations, cash flow, and financial condition.
quotes: While supply lead times have not fully returned to levels prior to the COVID-19 pandemic, FirstEnergy continues to monitor the situation in light of demand increases across the industry, including due to data center usage, and the imposition of tariffs and retaliatory tariffs that have been, and may be, imposed by the U.S. government in response.

a prolonged continuation or further increase in demand, or the continuation of uncertain or adverse macroeconomic conditions, including inflationary pressures and new or increased existing tariffs, could lead to an increase in supply chain disruptions that could, in turn, have an adverse effect on the Registrants' results of operations, cash flow and financial condition.
